explanation: While a dolphin sleeps, the waking side of its brain keeps it swimming, surfacing to breathe and watching for danger, and the eye linked to that side often stays open.

claims.text: Bottlenose dolphins sleep with each brain hemisphere in turn (unihemispheric sleep).
Giraffes, koalas and horses are not known to sleep with each brain hemisphere in turn.
During unihemispheric sleep, the awake hemisphere lets a dolphin keep swimming, surface to breathe and stay alert to danger.
During unihemispheric sleep, the eye controlled by the awake hemisphere often stays open.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: four listed, all standard. I wrote 'each side in turn' rather than 'one half', which keeps number words out of the key honestly. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology, so none applies and every high-risk claim needs web evidence from checker A. rivalTest: the distractors are animals famous for other sleep habits (giraffes sleep very little, koalas a lot, horses can doze standing up), so each tempts. Seals, manatees and many birds also sleep this way, which is why none of them is an option. Argued against the key: dolphins doing it is one of the best-documented cases. I swapped an earlier 'brown bear' distractor for the horse, because a claim naming koalas and bears together tripped the koalas-are-bears myth pattern. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: all four animals are known worldwide. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 30 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a multiple-choice item. doubts: c2 is worded 'not known to' because absence is hard to prove; I know of no record for any of the three.

evidence.restatement: Bottlenose dolphins show unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, resting one brain hemisphere at a time.
Unihemispheric sleep is known in cetaceans, eared seals, manatees and many birds, not in giraffes, horses or koalas.
The waking hemisphere keeps the dolphin swimming, surfacing to breathe and alert.
The eye controlled by the waking hemisphere (the opposite eye) tends to stay open.
Bottlenose dolphins sleep one brain hemisphere at a time (unihemispheric slow-wave sleep) and alternate sides.
Giraffes, koalas and horses sleep with both hemispheres; none is known for unihemispheric sleep.
The awake half keeps the dolphin swimming, surfacing to breathe and watching for danger.
The eye linked to the awake hemisphere often stays open.
